objectives.text: Stay out of other people's wars and keep the sultanate intact under Sultan Haitham: neutrality is not a posture but the survival strategy of a small Gulf state with Iran across the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia on its land border and the United States on its ports. The test of the doctrine is the 2026 Iran war, in which Oman condemned the US-Israeli strikes of 28 Feb ('undermining active and serious negotiations'), was itself hit by Iranian drones at Duqm, Salalah and Sohar, and still refused to join either camp.

grand_strategy.reading:
Oman in October 2026 is a neutral whose neutrality has been put under live fire.
Its whole strategy since Qaboos is to be useful to every side and enemy to none:
a venue for the Americans and the Iranians, a door to the Houthis, a berth for
the US, British and Indian navies, an oil seller to China, a land bridge for
the Gulf. The Iran war of 28 February 2026 tested each of those at once. Iranian
drones hit three Omani ports while Muscat was still hosting the talks, Trump
threatened twice to bomb the mediator, and the Hormuz deal Oman helped write
on 17 June was read by Tehran and Washington as two opposite things. Luttwak's
logic shows in that gap: the instruments of a small state's security (access,
mediation, a share of the Strait) are the same instruments that make it a
target and a suspect. What holds is that all sides still need Oman more than
they distrust it: the US needs a channel on Hormuz and the Houthis, Iran needs
the one Arab neighbour that answers its calls, the Saudis and Emiratis need a
southern flank that does not break. Signals that are not rows: the government
never answered Trump in public; Sultan Haitham flew to Abu Dhabi on 17 Aug,
the day of Trump's second threat, and to London on 2 July; the fiscal tax
reform of 2028 shows the leadership expects the oil rent to shrink. Open gaps in
this pass: Egypt, Jordan, Iraq, Pakistan, France and Russia (no sourced
reading yet), the exact terms of the Saudi road link, and a primary text for
the 2023 anti-normalisation measure.

stances.note: Not an alliance and not a client: Oman keeps Iran as the neighbour it must live with across the Strait of Hormuz and as the interlocutor no other Arab state can reach. Iran chose Oman as venue for the 2025 and Feb 2026 talks, Sultan Haitham was the first Arab leader to congratulate Mojtaba Khamenei (9 Mar 2026), Tehran pledged to double trade to USD 5bn (Sep 2025), and on 17 Aug 2026 the two announced an 'understanding' on a Hormuz transit map. Trend stable, not warming: Iranian drones hit Duqm, Salalah and Sohar in March 2026 and the IRGC struck Duqm on 12 Jul (Oman summoned the ambassador, 'irresponsible acts'), the worst crisis in decades per Iran International, which still calls Oman Iran's 'most valuable Arab partner'. Build warning (Iran grades Oman 'partner' while Oman has a treaty row with the US, which Iran grades adversary): answered - the 1980 and 2019 US texts are facilities-access agreements with no mutual-defence clause, Oman is bound by no defence treaty to Iran's enemies (the UK defence agreements aside), and Tehran itself chose Oman as venue for the 2025-26 talks. Bond affinity: decades of Qaboos-era contact and a shared Strait.

stances.note: The oldest Arab tie to Washington (Treaty of Amity and Commerce, 1833), formal US access since 1980 and Duqm and Salalah since 2019, a free trade agreement in force since 2009 - but no mutual-defence treaty, so 'partner' (transactional, no alignment) rather than ally. The grade is held back by the 2026 strain: Trump threatened Oman on 27 May ('behave ... or we will have to blow them up') and again in the week of 17 Aug; former ambassador Marc Sievers says Oman 'has not behaved as a neutral mediator'; Albusaidi wrote on 18 Mar that the US had 'lost control of its own foreign policy'. AGSI's Jacobs: the US 'needs Oman' on Hormuz. The 12 Jul IRGC strike on Duqm hit the US-facing facilities. Cooling, not broken. Bond affinity: two centuries of treaty relations and US training and arms, tempered by the Albusaidi criticism.
